description.narrative:
The overall objective of the UN Office of the High Commissioner of Human Rights (OHCHR) in Cambodia is to strengthen further the capacity of both governmental and non-governmental institutions to promote and protect human rights in Cambodia.
This objective will be achieved through four inter-connected goals:
- Advancing sustainable development through human rights - Strengthening rule of law and accountability for human rights violation - Increasing implementation of the outcomes of the international human rights mechanisms - Enhancing and protecting civic space and people's participation
The UN OHCHR in Cambodia aims at supporting the re-shaping of the pathway to sustainable development by strengthening its capacity for monitoring SDGs risk indicators, human rights mechanisms recommendations and tracking and reporting human rights violations and abuses. The OHCHR want to through its work in Cambodia improve UN´s prevention and early warning system and integrate a prevention agenda in UN´s development framework to improve the respect for human rigths and the achievement of the SDGs for Cambodia. The aim is to make Cambodia more resilient to crisis and make international development efforts more cost-efficient, save lives and safeguard development risks.
The intervention is focusing on the most disadvantaged groups facing high insecurities in their daily lives. These are the informal and migrant workers; indigenous communities and other ethnic minorities; persons with disabilities; LGBTI persons, youth, and elderly persons. Within all population in disadvantage or vulnerable situations referred to above women and girls are particularly marginalized - also evident in the Gender Inequality Index value where Cambodia rank 114 out of 162 countries.
The objective of the program is to strengthen the capacity of duty bearers and to promote and protect the human rights of the right holders - particularly the above identified groups that are most vulnerable and exposed in Cambodia.

Insatsen implementeras av FN´s högkommissionär för mänskliga rättigheter (OHCHR) genom dess landkontor i Kambodja. I partnerskap med OHCHR bidrar Sida till att stärka kapaciteten hos både statliga och icke-statliga aktörer för att främja och skydda mänskliga rättigheter som de uttrycks i internationell rätt och FN´s allmänna deklaration om de mänskliga rättigheterna.

The program is being implemented by the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) through its country office in Cambodia. In partnership with OHCHR, Sida contributes to strengthening the capacity of both state and non-state actors to promote and protect human rights as they are expressed in international law and in the UN Universal Declaration of Human Rights.

Monitoring & Protection
OHCHRs strengthened monitoring, reporting, and protection activities led to improvements in the documentation and response to human rights violations, especially in a context of shrinking civic space. Through continous monitoring of violations related to freedom of expression, association and peaceful assembly, OHCHR was able to bring increased national and international attention to these issues. Victim interviews, trial monitoring, and support for legal aid contributed to more informed advocacy and pressure on authorities for justice reform and respect for fair trial standards.
By conducting 26 visits to 11 prisons, OHCHR increased access to places of detention and built cooperative relationships with prison officials. This led to the launch of a pilot project in Kandal Provincial Prison in collaboration with the General Department of Prisons (GDP). OHCHR helped assess detention conditions and identify solutions to systemic challenges such as overcrowding. Access to detained human rights defenders and political actors also increased advocacy efforts towards national authorities and international mechanisms. In several instances, OHCHR support directly contributed to the release of detainees or to improvements in their detention conditions.
Civic Space & Participation
Despite increasing restrictions, OHCHRs continued to provide support to human rights defenders, media actors, and political actors. By securing releases in select cases, referring individuals to support services, and engaging with human rights mechanisms, OHCHR helped mitigate risks to civic actors and amplified their visibility.
Through capacity-building initiativesincluding targeted training on international human rights law, vulnerable group protections, and engagement with UN mechanismshuman rights actors enhanced their skills and confidence in upholding their rights. OHCHR also facilitated safe spaces for civil society and media to collaborate, discuss risks, and plan mitigation strategies, reinforcing their collective voice and resilience in a restrictive environment.
Mechanisms & Accountability
OHCHR played an important role in strengthening Cambodias engagement with international human rights mechanisms. In support of the Universal Periodic Review (UPR) 4th cycle, OHCHR provided technical assistance to the Cambodian Human Rights Committee (CHRC), coordinated UNCT inputs, and enabled civil society participation through technical and direct support. This included travel grants for 11 representatives of organizations for persons with disabilities (OPDs) to engage in UPR pre-sessions in Geneva, enhancing the inclusiveness and civil society voices..
OHCHRs support was important in advancing the governments finalization of the report to the Comittee of the Rights of Persons with Disability (CRPD) and promoting LGBTI rights through collaboration with the organisation Rainbow Community Kampuchea (RoCK)to implement recommendations by the UN Independent Expert on SOGI. Legal aid lawyers also improved their use of international human rights standards in court proceedings, particularly in cases involving freedom of expression. Trial monitoring and legal guidance provided by OHCHR led to stronger defenses and greater application of fair trial principles.
Technical Assistance
OHCHR's analysis of legal and policy frameworksincluding on the Law on Associations and NGOs (LANGO), alternative dispute resolution mechanisms, disability rights legislation, and the draft National Human Rights Commission lawfacilitated dialogue with authorities and encouraged reforms aligned with international norms. This engagement aimed to contribute to a growing institutional commitment to rights-based governance.
Capacity-building support targeted key state institutions such as the National Committee against Torture (NCAT), Ministry of Interior, Cambodian Human Rights Committee (CHRC), and Ministry of Social Affairs, Youth and Rehabilitation (MoSAVY). For example, training conducted with NCAT on torture prevention standards enhanced provincial officials' understanding and application of international human rights obligations, strengthening institutional responses to ill-treatment and detention conditions.
Partnerships with the United Nations Country Team (UNCT) and Communications
As leader of the UNCT Human Rights Group, OHCHR ensured the integration of a human rights-based approach into the UNs sustainability Development Cooperation Framework (UNSDCF) 20242028, incorporating human rights principles across all UN programming in Cambodia. Through communication, OHCHR enhanced the visibility and impact of its initiatives. Recognition from the EU external audit and OHCHR Gender Accreditation Programme confirmed the efforts of the OHCHRs outreach, particularly its success in stregthening the voices of marginalized groups including LGBTI people, Indigenous peoples, persons with disabilities, and women.
One result (Good Practice) example, including background and lessons learnt
Addressing the impacts of business activities on indigenous peoples human rights related to land Background: The Committee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights in its Concluding observations issued in 2023 was concerned by reports regarding the negative impacts that business activities and large development projects, including in the Special Economic Zones, have on the enjoyment of economic, social and cultural rights, in particular on access to land, the right to an adequate standard of living, labour rights and the right to health. The Committee was concerned that, while it is mandatory to carry out environmental impact assessments before realizing investments and implementing development projects, such assessments may not be carried out in an independent manner and in consultation with the relevant affected communities or groups.
OHCHR followed up on issues related to secure the equitable access to, use of and control over land by individuals and communities, especially indigenous peoples. State authorities have reportedly resorted to bringing criminal charges against members of communities in a vulnerable situation, or have refrained from issuing land titles as a form of intimidation. OHCHR received information of attempts to evict vulnerable communities, including Indigenous communities, from their lands without meaningful consultation, or transparent and fair agreements on resettlement, or compensation. In some situations, land petitions by representatives of Indigenous communities to the State authorities have been kept pending. In other instances, Indigenous communities have not been issued with collective land titles for lands or portions of their lands that have been allocated as economic concessions to private companies without prior consultation and compensation, thus denying the Indigenous communities affected access to their lands and enjoyment of their rights.
Result: OHCHR published a Study on the Human Rights Situation of Communities Living in Resettlement Sites in Cambodia and developed Draft Resettlement Guidelines, which addressed the relocation of Indigenous peoples. These tools provided evidence and recommendations that have informed both national and international discussions on resettlement practices, contributing to advancing the protection standards for affected communities. OHCHR supported Indigenous peoples in making formal submissions to UN Special Procedures regarding alleged violations of their land and housing rights. This support enhanced Indigenous communities access to international human rights mechanisms and increased their concerns to the global level, contributing to holding duty-bearers accountable. OHCHR played an important role in supporting the United Nations Country Team to analyze amendments to the Law on Natural Protected Areas and submitting these recommendations to the Government. This intervention contributed to the ongoing legislative review aimed at aligning Cambodian law with international human rights obligations particularly the recognition of Indigenous peoples land tenure systems and collective ownership rights.
Lessons and success factors related to this example: Greater transparency is needed in the planning, implementation, and assessment of Special Economic Zones where business are involved concerning use of land. This includes full disclosure of the impacts on land rights, local communities, workers rights, and the environment, as well as clear information on the tax and investment incentives and the remedies available for rights violations.
States must uphold the principle of FPIC (Free, Prior and Informed Consent) in all matters affecting Indigenous peoples, particularly in relation to land and resource use. Respect for this principle is fundamental to upholding Indigenous sovereignty and autonomy.
The impact of business activities on Indigenous peoples' land access must be a core component of human rights impact assessments and/or environmental safeguards. Ignoring these impacts undermines Indigenous rights and risks causing harm.
